blocks.text: Re-ranker fine-tuning trains a model to take the candidate documents an initial retrieval stage, covered in the previous topic, already narrowed down, and produce a more precise final ranking, typically using the cross-encoder architecture briefly introduced in that same topic.

This topic covers why re-ranking exists as a distinct second stage, how cross-encoder training data differs from the retrieval training data covered previously, and the latency tradeoff that shapes when re-ranking is worth the extra cost.
1. What Re-Ranker Fine-Tuning Targets

blocks.alt: A candidate set from retrieval goes through a fine-tuned re-ranker, producing a refined ranking

blocks.text: Re-ranker fine-tuning teaches a model to take the relatively small candidate set an initial retrieval stage already surfaced and reorder it more precisely, focusing all its capacity on distinguishing among documents that are already broadly relevant rather than searching a full large collection.
2. Two-Stage Retrieval and Re-Ranking

blocks.alt: A fast first stage retrieval is followed by a precise second stage re-ranking

blocks.text: The two stages covered across this and the previous topic exist because of the speed and accuracy tradeoff between bi-encoder and cross-encoder architectures, covered in the previous topic, retrieval quickly narrows a huge collection down using the cheap bi-encoder, re-ranking then applies the more expensive but more accurate cross-encoder only to that much smaller candidate set.
3. Cross-Encoder Training Data

blocks.alt: Query text and document text form a joint cross-encoder input, producing a relevance score

blocks.text: Unlike the bi-encoder training covered in the previous topic, which embeds query and document separately, cross-encoder training data feeds the query and a candidate document together as a single joint input, and the model directly outputs a relevance score for that specific pairing.
4. Scoring Candidates, Not the Full Collection

blocks.alt: Scoring every document in the collection is compared against scoring only top candidates from retrieval

blocks.text: Because cross-encoder scoring is computationally expensive per document pair, it is applied only to the top candidates an initial retrieval stage already surfaced, typically a few dozen documents, rather than the full collection, which could be millions of documents, this candidate-narrowing role is exactly what makes the two-stage pipeline practical.

blocks.text: 5. Pairwise vs Listwise Ranking Data

blocks.alt: Pairwise ranked data compared against a listwise ranked list

blocks.text: Re-ranker training data can be structured as pairwise comparisons, this document is more relevant than that one, similar in spirit to the preference pairs covered in the earlier Alignment Training module, or as a full listwise ranking of several candidates for one query, listwise data generally gives the model more complete ranking signal per training example.

blocks.title: This mirrors the DPO versus other alignment method data tradeoffs
blocks.content: Just as different alignment training methods covered earlier in this course use different data shapes, pairwise and listwise ranking data each shape what the re-ranker learns and how much labeling effort each training example requires.

blocks.text: 6. The Latency Tradeoff

blocks.alt: Re-ranker latency is compared against retrieval only latency

blocks.text: Adding a re-ranking stage improves final ranking quality but adds latency, every production system needs to weigh this tradeoff, a search feature where users expect near instant results may accept retrieval-only ranking, one where result quality matters more than shaving off milliseconds often benefits from the added re-ranking stage.
7. Re-Ranking Within a Full RAG Pipeline

blocks.alt: Retrieval is followed by re-ranking, then generation

blocks.text: In a retrieval augmented generation pipeline, covered in the earlier RAG course, re-ranking commonly sits between the initial retrieval stage and the final generation step, ensuring the documents actually passed to the generating model are the most relevant ones available, not just the broadly relevant candidate set retrieval alone produced.
8. Evaluating Re-Rankers

Re-ranker evaluation uses the same retrieval-specific metrics covered in the previous topic, recall at K, MRR, and NDCG, but computed specifically on the re-ranked output, comparing these metrics before and after re-ranking directly quantifies how much value the added stage provides for a given use case.
9. When Re-Ranking Is Worth the Added Cost

Re-ranking tends to be worth its added latency and compute cost specifically when initial retrieval quality alone leaves meaningful room for improvement, and when the downstream use, a generation step or a user facing ranked list, is sensitive to getting the very top results exactly right.
Worked Example

A team running a retrieval augmented generation pipeline for customer support finds that responses sometimes cite a document that is topically related but not the most directly relevant one available, even though a more relevant document was present in the initial retrieval candidates.

Adding a fine-tuned cross-encoder re-ranking stage between retrieval and generation, trained on pairwise relevance comparisons, measurably improves NDCG on their evaluation set and reduces this citation mismatch, at the cost of a modest latency increase they determine is acceptable given how much the answer quality improved.
Common Mistakes

items: Applying a cross-encoder re-ranker directly to a full large collection instead of a narrowed candidate set from retrieval
Not measuring the actual latency cost of re-ranking against the ranking quality improvement it provides
Using retrieval-only evaluation metrics without checking whether re-ranking meaningfully improves them
Training a re-ranker on only easy pairwise comparisons, missing the finer relevance distinctions harder comparisons would teach

blocks.text: Practice

For a retrieval pipeline you are familiar with or could imagine, decide whether adding a re-ranking stage would likely be worth its added latency, using the tradeoff covered in this topic, and if so, sketch what a pairwise training example for that re-ranker would look like.
Key Takeaway

Re-ranker fine-tuning trains a cross-encoder model to precisely reorder the small candidate set an initial retrieval stage, covered in the previous topic, already narrowed down, trading added latency for improved ranking quality, and it commonly sits between retrieval and generation in a full RAG pipeline, evaluated using the same recall at K, MRR, and NDCG metrics applied specifically to the re-ranked output.
